justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 518.5 was anchored heavily to recent price action and short-term momentum, with very little deviation expected over such a brief window. The one-week estimate of 522 incorporated a slight bullish lean, possibly reflecting trend continuation or a stable macro backdrop, while the one-month estimate of 530 extended that drift further, consistent with a long-run tendency for equity-linked instruments or broadly traded assets to grind higher in the absence of major shocks. The gradual step-up across horizons reflects mean drift assumptions rather than any strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths expand significantly as the horizon lengthens, and this is by design. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 41 points, which reflects normal intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, that band grows to 80 points, accounting for the accumulation of daily variance and the possibility of a meaningful news event. At one month, the interval widens to 180 points, acknowledging that over four weeks, macro data releases, central bank communications, earnings, and geopolitical developments can all compound to produce substantial moves in either direction. The scaling broadly follows a square-root-of-time logic applied to typical realized volatility.

The main sources of uncertainty beyond normal statistical variance include shifts in monetary policy expectations, particularly any surprise in inflation data or central bank tone that could reprice rate expectations sharply. Liquidity conditions, positioning extremes, and any deterioration in credit markets or earnings guidance could also amplify moves. On the upside, stronger-than-expected economic data or a dovish pivot could push prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval.

Tail risks that could push outcomes entirely outside my stated intervals include a sudden geopolitical escalation, a financial system stress event such as a large institutional failure, or an unexpected policy shock like emergency rate changes. These are low-probability but fat-tail events that by construction a 90% interval does not fully contain. A black swan of sufficient magnitude could easily produce a move two or three times the width of my stated one-month range, and this remains the most important caveat to interpreting any of these estimates as reliable bounds rather than probabilistic guides.
